titleStmt.title: Exact schedulability analysis for single-rate periodic cyclic executives for a refined system model

analytic.title: Exact schedulability analysis for single-rate periodic cyclic executives for a refined system model

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Despite their industrial relevance, contemporary textbooks hardly address cyclic executives, if at all. There is therefore a need for analysis techniques for these executives.

Earlier work considered exact schedulabilily analysis of basic single-rate cyclic executives for a basic system model. In this paper, we present exact schedulability analysis of a single-rate periodic cyclic executive, for a refined model in which the notion of observable event [1] is taken into account. We compare the single-rate periodic cyclic executive with the single-rate AFAP (as fast as possible) and single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executives from a scheduling perspective for this refined model.

div.head: A. Background and motivation
div.p: Since the paper of C. Douglass Locke [2], in which it was concluded that the fixed-priority approach generally dominates the cyclic executive approach for hard real-time systems, the academic interest in cyclic executives has gradually decreased. As a result, cyclic executives are mentioned in contemporary text books, such as [3]- [6], but hardly addressed in detail. In a recent survey of 120 industry practitioners in the field of real-time embedded systems [7], it was observed that from the 97 respondents to the question which task scheduling policy/policies are used in the considered systems, 54.17% answered "static cycle/table driven/time-triggered", amongst other policies. Given their industrial relevance, proper explanation of cyclic executives and their analysis therefore remains desirable.

div.head: B. Problem description
div.p: Hard real-time systems require timely responses to events. In this paper, we assume a hard real-time system with a set of n (input) events, a set of n (output) responses, and a 1-1 relationship between events and responses. Events are sporadic, i.e. are characterized by a minimal inter-arrival time. Each event-response tuple is characterized by a bestcase and a worst-case system deadline, where the worst-case system deadline is at most equal to the minimal inter-arrival time of the event. Each event-response tuple is handled by a dedicated real-time polling task, which detects the event (through regularly polling a sensor) and provides a response (using an actuator). We assume a single-processor system and a basic single-rate cyclic executive to schedule the set of tasks.

In earlier work, we presented exact analysis for basic singlerate cyclic executives [8], [9] for a basic real-time system model. Moreover, we presented analysis for single-rate AFAP (as fast as possible) and single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executives for a refined model [10] in which the notion of observable event [1] is taken into account. Analysis for a single-rate periodic cyclic executive for that refined model has not yet been addressed, however.

div.head: C. Contributions
div.p: In this paper, we present exact analysis for single-rate periodic cyclic executives for a refined model in which the notion of observable event [1] is taken into account and the 1-1 correspondence between events and responses is exploited. In addition, the single-rate periodic cyclic executive is compared to the single-rate AFAP and single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executives from a scheduling perspective.

div.head: D. Organization
div.p: The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Section II, the basic model and the refined model are recapitulated. Section III recapitulates basic single-rate cyclic executives. The worst-case schedulability analysis for a singlerate periodic cyclic executive is addressed in Section IV. A comparison from a scheduling perspective of the cyclic executives as well as the models is the topic of Section V. The paper is concluded in Section VI.

div.head: II. RECAP OF REAL-TIME SYSTEM MODELS
div.p: In this section, the basic model M B presented in [8] and the refined model M R presented in [10] are recapitulated.

div.head: A. A basic real-time system model M B
div.p: We assume a system S, a set E S of n sporadic (input) events e 1 , e 2 , . . . , e n , a set R S of n (output) responses r 1 , r 2 , . . . , r n to these events, and a 1-1 relationship between events and responses. Each event e i is characterized by a minimal interarrival time WT S i . Each event-response tuple e i , r i is characterized by a best-case system deadline BD S i and a worst-case system deadline WD S i , where 0 ≤ BD S i ≤ WD S i ≤ WT S i . Moreover, we assume a set T S of n independent, 'regularly' polling tasks τ 1 , τ 2 , . . . , τ n , where task τ i senses event e i and provides response r i . Each task τ i is characterized by a bestcase computation time BC i and a worst-case computation time WC i , where 0 < BC i ≤ WC i . The execution of a task is termed a job. A job of task τ i is denoted by ι i,k , with 0 ≤ k, i.e. the first job of τ i is denoted by ι i,0 . The computation time C i,k of every job ι i,k of task τ i shall be between BC i and WC i , i.e.
div.formula: ∀ 1≤i≤n ∧ 0≤k BC i ≤ C i,k ≤ WC i .
div.p: We use s i,k and f i,k to denote the start time and the finalization time of job ι i,k , respectively. For ease of presentation and without loss of generality, the jobs of tasks in a cycle are assumed to be executed in the order of increasing index, i.e.
div.formula: ∀ 1≤i<j≤n ∧ 0≤k s i,k < s j,k . B. A refined real-time system model M R
div.p: The basic real-time systems model can be refined by taking the notion of observable event [1] 1 into account. The last observable event of a task (in our case a response) need not be at the end of a task's execution. Moreover, a job of a task does not necessarily provide a response, i.e. given the 1-1 correspondence between events and responses, there will be no response when a job does not detect an event.
To address these two aspects, the model can be refined by distinguishing additional notions of best-case and worst-case computation times of a task τ i , e.g.
• BC r i and WC r i : the best-case and worst-case computation time for task τ i to provide a response, respectively;
• BC nr i and WC nr i : the best-case and worst-case computation time when no response is given (i.e. no event is detected) by τ i . For these additional notions, we assume 2

div.head: III. RECAP OF SINGLE-RATE CYCLIC EXECUTIVES
div.p: For (basic) cyclic executives, tasks can simply be implemented as procedures and executed within a loop. A singlerate cyclic executive essentially executes every task exactly once in a cycle. In the following subsections, three basic types of single-rate cyclic executives are recapitulated, AFAP, timedriven AFAP, and periodic.

div.head: A. Single-rate AFAP cyclic executive
div.p: Figure 1 illustrates a single-rate AFAP cyclic executive. Note that the processor is constantly busy executing tasks.

div.head: B. Single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive
div.p: For a single-rate time-driven AFAP, a cycle is started by a timer. The sum of the worst-case computation times of all tasks shall be less than the inter-arrival time T S of the timer, otherwise the (worst-case) executions of the tasks do not 'fit' in a cycle, i.e.
div.formula: 1≤i≤n WC i ≤ T S .
div.p: Figure 2 illustrates a single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive with cycle time T S , where the cycle is started at time Φ.

div.head: C. Single-rate periodic cyclic executive
div.p: Similar to the single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive, the tasks shall 'fit' in a cycle, i.e. (5) shall hold. Figure 3 illustrates such a single-rate periodic cyclic executive with cycle time T S , where every task is started at a specific time.
In particular, we assume that every task is started at the worstcase start-time relative to the start of the cycle assuming each task needs its worst-case computation time.

div.head: IV. WORST-CASE ANALYSIS FOR M R
div.p: In this section, we first recapitulate exact conditions for the schedulability of a system S when tasks are scheduled by a basic cyclic executive for the refined model M R . We subsequently present example systems, which we will use in the remainder of the section for illustration purposes. Next, we recapitulate the analysis for the single-rate AFAP and singlerate time-driven cyclic executive and present the exact analysis for the single-rate periodic cyclic executive.

div.head: V. COMPARISON OF CYCLIC EXECUTIVES AND MODELS
div.p: In this section, we compare the single-rate periodic cyclic executive with the single-rate AFAP and single-rate timedriven AFAP cyclic executives from a scheduling perspective. Moreover, we compare the analysis for basic model M B and the refined model M R .

div.head: A. AFAP dominates periodic
div.p: We will prove that the single-rate AFAP cyclic executive dominates the single-rate periodic cyclic executive from a scheduling perspective for the refined model M R , whereas these two cyclic executives are equivalent for the basic model M B ; see Theorem 4. We now first present a lemma stating that if a system is schedulable under a single-rate periodic cyclic executive for M R , then it will also be schedulable under a single rate AFAP cyclic executive.

div.head: B. Periodic dominates time-driven AFAP
div.p: In this section, we will prove that the single-rate periodic cyclic executive dominates the single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive from a scheduling perspective for the refined model M R , similar to the basic model M B ; see [9]. Lemma 2. When a system S is schedulable under a singlerate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive for our refined model M R , it is also schedulable under a single-rate periodic cyclic executive.

Proof. Based on (1) -( 4), we derive ∀ 1≤i≤n BC i ≤ WC i . As a result, (8) implies (9), which concludes the proof. Theorem 6. From a scheduling perspective, the single-rate periodic cyclic executive dominates the single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive for our refined model M R .
Proof. Follows immediately from Lemma 2 and example system S II .

div.head: C. Analysis based on M R dominates analysis based on M B
div.p: In [10], it was proven that the refined model M R dominates the basic model M B from a scheduling perspective for both the single-rate AFAP as well as the single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive. As expressed by the following theorem, which we present without proof for reasons of space, the same holds for the single-rate periodic cyclic executive. Theorem 7. From a scheduling perspective, the refined model M R dominates the basic model M B for the single-rate periodic cyclic executive.
We therefore conclude that the refined model M R dominates the basic model M B from a scheduling perspective for the basic single-rate cyclic executives considered.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSION
div.p: In this paper, we considered scheduling of independent, 'regularly' polling tasks on a single processor using a singlerate periodic cyclic executive for a refined model M R in which the notion of observable event [1] is taken into account and the 1-1 correspondence between events and responses is exploited.

We presented exact analysis for single-rate periodic cyclic executives for M R . Because best-case analysis turned out to be trivial, focus of this paper has been on exact worst-case analysis (Theorem 3). Our analysis derives feasible cycle times of a single-rate periodic cyclic executive for a system. We subsequently compared the single-rate periodic cyclic executive with the single-rate AFAP and single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executives from a schedulability perspective for M R . In particular, we provided two schedulability related proofs. We first proved that the single-rate AFAP cyclic executive dominates the single-rate periodic cyclic executive (Theorem 5). This came as a surprise for two reasons. Firstly, the two cyclic executives are equivalent from a scheduling perspective for the basic model M B ; see [9]. Secondly, the worst-case analysis is pessimistic for the AFAP cyclic executive, whereas it is exact for the periodic cyclic executive. We next proved that the single-rate periodic cyclic executive dominates the single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive (Theorem 6), as is also the case for M B ; see [9]. Finally, we presented a theorem stating that M R dominates M B from a scheduling perspective for the basic single-rate cyclic executives considered (Theorem 7).

As future work, we aim at a further extension of our real-time system model by taking the single-path code paradigm [12]- [14] into account, in particular to support timedeterministic communication in a networked context.
